subjects.introduction: Sleep and waking, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá observes, are what the body’s own essential relationships require of it at different hours; and such relationships, He says, run through every created thing as a divine trust. Nature itself is nothing other than the necessary relations inherent in the realities of things, each reality a requisite of every other, the whole held in order by an unseen unifying power, as the body is held by the mind. From this follow large claims: that religion consists in those same necessary relationships, that divine law is the resolution of truth, reason and justice rather than an imposition of will, and that peace depends on a constellation of connected matters rather than any single one. Marcus Aurelius, meditating on the connection of all things, reasons from a Stoic cosmos toward practical attention [1]; the Bahá’í teaching asks what such connectedness obliges us to do, and warns that human intelligence alone cannot encompass it. The journey leads on to interconnectedness, to the law of cause and effect, and to the question of what religion really is.
subjects.arc: Begin with familiar rhythms, follow their connections into nature and ethics, and ask what interdependence requires of us.

order.why: Widen the view to the connections within nature. Develop the picture of reciprocal action throughout creation.
shortened: Now concerning nature, it is but the essential properties and the necessary relations inherent in the realities of things. And though these infinite realities are diverse in their character yet they are in the utmost harmony and closely connected together. As one's vision is broadened and the matter observed carefully, it will be made certain that every reality is but an essential requisite of other realities. Thus to connect and harmonize these diverse and infinite realities an all-unifying Power is necessary, that every part of existent being may in perfect order discharge its own function.

order.why: Begin with relationships as a trust, using sleep and waking as familiar examples.
Connect those relationships to the conditions of lasting peace.
Connects alteration in necessary relationships with the continual transformation of the contingent world.
Introduce the moral judgments available to reason.
shortened: But the divine philosophers hold that the excellence or baseness of things depends upon both reason and religious law. Thus, the prohibitions on murder, theft, treachery, falsehood, hypocrisy, and iniquity are based on reason: Every rational mind can grasp that these are all vile and reprehensible. For if you merely prick a man with a thorn he will cry out in pain: How well must he realize then that murder, according to reason, is vile and reprehensible.

order.why: Examine the grounding of law in truth and justice.
shortened: 'The Laws of God are not imposition of will, or of power, or pleasure, but the resolutions of truth, reason and justice.'

order.why: Return the idea of order to responsibility for our effects upon it.
Distinguish natural processes from the ideals of the Kingdom.
Defines fate and predestination through necessary relationships and distinguishes the role of will.
Consider religious guidance in relation to changing human conditions.
shortened: Briefly, the universal Manifestations of God are aware of the truths underlying the mysteries of all created things, and thus they found a religion that is based upon and consonant with the prevailing condition of humanity. For religion consists in the necessary relationships deriving from the realities of things.

order.why: Place law within the requirements of associated life.
shortened: For the true Order and Law are those inherent properties and necessary conditions in the realities of things, and the essence of existing realities needs these relations.

If thou canst promote this order and organization and this heavenly Law so that thou mayest truly become organizer of the spiritual souls and the arranger of the pearls of the mercy of the All-Merciful One.

order.why: End with a historical claim that tests the limits of inference from relationships.
shortened: However, some among the ancients through the power of detachment gained knowledge of certain cosmic mysteries and obtained awareness of relationships and connections that exist between created things - they became aware of certain hidden secrets in the realities of things and deduced some future events from the relationships between existing things. This cannot be denied, as mentioned in the Kitab-i-Iqan regarding the brilliant star that indicated the birth of Christ. But the superstitions contained in astrological books are absolutely not to be trusted.

order.why: Explore the limits of unaided human understanding.
Draw out the connection between social order and happiness.

questions: How does seeing relationships as a trust change the way we understand an ordinary activity or obligation?
What additional reasoning is needed to move from the way nature works to the way people ought to treat one another?
Why might peace depend on a constellation of relationships and shared understandings rather than a single measure?
How could an awareness of interdependence deepen inquiry while leaving room to question particular predictions?

neighbors.invitation: Explore the competing lessons people draw from cooperation and struggle in nature.
Bring a vision of human interdependence into specific acts of service.

references.label: 1 · Marcus Aurelius, Meditations VI.38
references.note: Find the meditation beginning with the connection of all things. Marcus grounds this connection in his Stoic account of the cosmos. Compare the practical attention he encourages with the compilation’s discussion of necessary relationships, without assuming that their accounts of God and nature are identical.

subjects.introduction: Ask why a chair exists and there are four honest answers. A carpenter made it, wood gives it body, its shape makes it a chair, and it exists so that someone may sit. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá uses this homely example to name the efficient, material, formal and final causes on which every created thing depends. Beside them He sets another triad, knowledge, volition and action, without which nothing is ever accomplished, as anyone who has tried to build a house soon discovers. The Báb carries the same fourfold pattern into the highest reaches of creation, where even the First Remembrance exists through the creative act of God, its very being, its form, and its fruit. Aristotle, who first sorted the meanings of why in this way, makes a natural companion [1]. To ask about causes is finally to ask about dependence and purpose: what holds a thing in being, and what it is for. The inquiry leads on to the law of cause and effect, to matter, essence and form, and to the purposeful motion that runs through all creation.
subjects.arc: Start with a chair, distinguish kinds of explanation, and follow causal language into questions of creation and purpose.

order.why: Make the four causes concrete through the construction of a chair.
Distinguish knowledge, volition, and action from the fourfold analysis.
shortened: The attainment of any object is conditioned upon knowledge, volition and action. Unless these three conditions are forthcoming, there is no execution or accomplishment. In the erection of a house it is first necessary to know the ground, and design the house suitable for it; second, to obtain the means or funds necessary for the construction; third, actually to build it.

order.why: An explicit account of all four causal roles and their application to the author’s theological framework.
Relates all four causes to the four elements and explains the final cause through the station of the Shia.
Restate the four causes before their theological application.
Encounter the more compressed symbolic use of the framework.

questions: How would the four kinds of explanation illuminate something you make, an institution you belong to, or a practice you value?
What does the distinction between knowing, willing, and acting add to an account of how things come about?
When causal language moves from an artifact to creation as a whole, which features of the analogy remain helpful and which need reconsideration?

neighbors.invitation: Explore causal dependence and the distinction between essential and temporal origination.
Consider how explanation changes when things are understood through their relationships.

references.label: 1 · Aristotle, Physics II.3
references.note: In Part 3, Aristotle distinguishes material, form, the source of change, and the end for which something occurs. Read his examples beside the chair. How does allowing several answers to “why” enrich an explanation, and how might an analogy become misleading?

subjects.introduction: A young man whose father has died in war can say to himself that God is his Father and that this Fatherhood is eternal; ‘Abdu’l-Bahá offers that consolation without hesitation. He also warns that whole peoples have pictured a god in their minds and bow before a fancy of their own contriving, since whatever the mind comprehends is smaller than the mind. Both are true, and the question of a personal God lives in the tension between them. Personality, He writes, belongs to the Manifestation of the Divinity, not to the Essence, which is remote, limitless, and impersonal; the worship Christ asks for is the worship of His attributes, not of His person. Even the wrath of God is reread as justice, the moment when a fatherly embrace gives way to a businesslike accounting because we have withdrawn. The Qur’an says that nothing is like God and in the same verse that He hears and sees [1], affirming qualities while refusing a likeness. Prayer can stay intimate while its picture of the One addressed remains open to correction. The inquiry leads on to God as immanent and transcendent, to the relationship of the Manifestation to God, and to the unknowability that keeps every image provisional.
subjects.arc: Enter through consolation, question our mental pictures, and explore intimacy with a reality beyond our categories.

order.why: Challenge the sufficiency of the image the mind creates.
shortened: This people, all of them, have pictured a god in the realm of the mind, and worship that image which they have made for themselves.

Consider then, how all the peoples of the world are bowing the knee to a fancy of their own contriving, how they have created a creator within their own minds, and they call it the Fashioner of all that is -- whereas in truth it is but an illusion. Thus are the people worshipping only an error of perception.

order.why: Interprets the image of God through knowledge, life, power, will and love, offering an account in terms of attributes.
Argues explicitly for intelligence, comprehension and volition in the Creator rather than an uncomprehending cause.
Distinguish the Manifestation’s personality from the divine Essence.
shortened: Thou hast written concerning the Impersonality of the Divinity. Personality is in the Manifestation of the Divinity, not in the Essence of the Divinity.

order.why: Close with the limits of personal and impersonal categories.
shortened: The Divine Reality is far removed from man. It is absolutely remote and independent in its essence - beyond the comprehension of man - abstract, limitless and impersonal.

order.why: Directly contrasts an impersonal, unmoving first cause with a freely acting Creator.
Begin with the human need for consolation and the image of a Father.
shortened: The axis around which the consolation of the hearts revolve is the Faith in God. If the father of a youth who believes in God is killed in the war - he will say to himself I have God for my father, whose Fatherhood is eternal. He is the Comforter of the broken-hearted ones. The miraculous power of Faith will cheer them up and heal their wounds.

order.why: Consider devotion directed toward the divine qualities revealed in Christ.
shortened: "The epitome of all worship is the worship of the attributes of Christ, not his personality."

order.why: Examine personal and objective language about divine anger.
Complicate an easy spatial account of divine presence.

questions: What makes a relationship with God personal in these passages, and what meanings of personality do they resist?
How can an image console us without becoming the boundary of what we are willing to understand?
What changes when words such as anger or presence are read through the distinction between the divine Essence and its manifestations?

neighbors.invitation: Examine how a mental picture may become a veil.
Follow the image of the mirror into the question of what can be known of God.

references.label: 1 · Qur’an 42:11 — incomparability and divine attributes
references.note: The verse denies a likeness to God while attributing hearing and seeing to Him. Compare this combination with the compilation’s use of personal language. How can a text affirm meaningful qualities while resisting a human likeness? Several translations make the interpretive choices visible.

subjects.displayTitle: Beyond a human image of God
subjects.introduction: Every mind that reaches toward God carries a picture, and the picture can become the problem. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá speaks of those who assigned God attributes, a spiritual identity and a form out of their own imaginings, and who, when reality failed to match, stayed behind the veil they had woven. The Bahá’í writings press this further into a sharp disagreement with Christian teaching: the Báb refuses the idea that the Divine Essence can be a Son in any literal sense, and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá denies that the incomprehensible Reality was embodied, suffered and died, since hardship belongs to this plane and the Almighty stands sanctified above it. These are arguments from one religious standpoint and should be weighed as such, which is why John’s prologue repays a direct reading, holding the Word made flesh beside the statement that no one has seen God [1]. The question underneath is how far language borrowed from human life can carry spiritual meaning before it hardens into an idol, and that question opens onto symbolism, the transcendence of God, and the limits of what any creature can know of Him.
subjects.arc: Question the image we form, encounter a theological disagreement, and return to the work of understanding another tradition on its own terms.

order.why: Begin with the general problem of mistaking an imagined form for God.
Answers a concrete question about He is God and the danger of worshipping mental images.
Quoted tradition explains why literal descriptions impose limits on God.
Concise contrast between divine attributes and bodily instruments or processes.
Explains hearing and sight as divine names without bodily limitations.
Explains divine attributes as denial of imperfections rather than humanly conceived qualities.
Distinguishes the vision of the heart from physical sight of God.
Interprets the image and likeness of God as virtues rather than a human shape.
Distinguishes the hidden Essence from names and attributes revealed through the Prophets.
Directly distinguishes manifestation from transformation of divinity into human nature.
Explains the Father in the Son through reflection rather than bodily entry.
Move into a particular critique of divine embodiment.
Read the Báb’s argument about sonship after establishing its theological concern.

questions: How might we distinguish a fruitful religious image from a conception that limits what we can recognize?
What becomes clearer, and what remains in disagreement, when these critiques are read alongside John’s own language about the Word and the unseen God?
How do the explanations of hearing, sight, and reflection help distinguish divine attributes from bodily processes?

neighbors.invitation: Place the criticism of human images beside the consoling language of divine fatherhood.
Consider the relation between the vessel of a word and the meaning it carries.

references.label: 1 · John 1:1–18 — the Word and the unseen God
references.note: Read especially verses 14 and 18 together. The Christian text supplies its own account of revelation and incarnation, allowing a comparison with the compilation’s objections. Give particular attention to what a fair statement of each position needs to preserve.

subjects.introduction: Not a leaf stirs without God knowing its movement, Bahá’u’lláh says, and the secrets of hearts are engraved in clear characters before Him. Being known that completely raises the old anxiety at once: if my deed is known before I do it, am I still free? ‘Abdu’l-Bahá answers that knowledge is not the cause of what it knows. The gardener knows which fruit will be bitter without making it so, and the astronomer who predicts an eclipse does not cause one; God’s knowledge, freed from past and future, encompasses all things without producing them. The harder puzzle is that our words for time and multiplicity hardly apply to the divine Essence at all. Psalm 139 approaches the same subject from inside prayer, where being searched and known is a comfort rather than a threat [1]. The teaching turns practical in two directions: an unseen moral life asks for integrity, and since all knowledge is divine knowledge and every creature a sign of God’s power, no one may look on another with contempt. The road continues into the attributes of God, into knowledge itself, and into the recognition of God.
subjects.arc: Begin with intimate awareness, investigate foreknowledge and freedom, and return to the ethics of being fully known.

order.why: Distinguish knowing an outcome from causing it through the gardener.
Begin with the vivid image of a leaf whose movement is known.
shortened: Likewise the Surih of Heykal and others like it, that thou mayest know of a certainty that not a leaf stirreth except that God knoweth its movement, its stability and its conditions.

order.why: Turn from the visible world to the secrets of the heart. Bring the discussion to concealed conduct and accountability.
Introduce knowledge that precedes and follows events.
Develop the distinction through the eclipse analogy and the limits of human time. Retain the separate formulation as a chance to reconsider the argument.
shortened: Answer: The knowledge of a thing is not the cause of its occurrence; for the essential knowledge of God encompasses the realities of all things both before and after they come to exist, but it is not the cause of their existence. This is an expression of the perfection of God.

Through astronomical calculations the mathematicians determine that at a certain time a solar or lunar eclipse will occur. Surely this prediction is not the cause of the eclipse. This of course is merely an analogy and not an exact image.

order.why: Pause over the relation between divine knowledge and its objects.
shortened: Created things were known to God, but the name "All-Seeing" had no connection to the realities of things. When they became realized in the world of existence, the name "All-Seeing" connected with them.

order.why: Affirms that nothing escapes divine knowledge and that all things are encompassed by it.
State the foreknowledge question directly.
Connect knowledge with patience and forbearance.
Consider the difficulty of attributing multiplicity to the Essence.
shortened: In truth, knowledge of multiplicities holds no nobility in the station of the Essence; rather it is polytheism according to the people of glory, for in the station of knowledge of the Essence, every mention of anything is invalid and indeed indicates polytheism and imperfection.

The nobility among the people of the Bayan and glory in the station of existences and entities is pure simplicity in the station of the manifestation of the Essence. Otherwise, attachment to multiplicities and knowledge of them is imperfection for one who knows the wisdom of the manifestations of the Divine Essence in the Kingdom of Names and Attributes.

order.why: End with the ethical consequence of recognizing divine signs in every person.
shortened: In brief, it means that all knowledge is divine knowledge, meaning realities must be known for knowledge to be realized - until something is encompassed, the encompasser cannot encompass it. And all creation manifests signs of God's might and power. In this light, one cannot consider people as ignorant while counting oneself as learned, for knowledge of truth is divine knowledge - knowledge is identical with what is known. And all created things are signs of power - one cannot look with contempt upon divine signs.

order.why: Encounter a more technical account of knowledge, will, and realization.
shortened: The truth is that when the creative action is related to existence, it is the Will; when it is related to the archetype ('ayn), in other words, the species form, it is Purpose; and when it is related to the limitations of the created, that is to say, their topography (handasa)--which includes length and breadth, continuance and mortality, term of duration, and the like--it is predestination. Through the accomplishment of the act of creation and the thing itself, it is fate; and through its manifestation, the revealing of causes, and the disclosure of means, it is execution....

questions: How do the gardener and eclipse comparisons distinguish knowledge from causation, and where do their limits matter?
What assumptions about time enter the question of whether foreknowledge removes freedom?
How might the experience of being fully known deepen both accountability and trust?
Why could reflection on divine knowledge lead to greater respect for people whose inner lives we do not know?

neighbors.invitation: Examine the distinction between an object in thought and an existent reality.
Follow recognition of a common humanity into the manner of teaching and meeting others.

references.label: 1 · Psalm 139:1–12 — the known and searching heart
references.note: The psalm places intimate knowledge beside a presence from which the speaker cannot flee. Compare its devotional treatment with the compilation’s philosophical distinction between knowing and causing. What can prayer express about this subject that an argument leaves open?

subjects.introduction: A mirror can hold the sun’s image without holding the sun. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá uses that commonplace to reconcile two convictions: the divine Essence lies beyond every mind, and God can nevertheless be known. We know Him, he says, by His attributes, His signs and His names, scattered as traces through the universe, and we know Him most fully in the Manifestation, the mirror held before the Sun in which all its perfections appear, so that knowledge of the Manifestations is the knowledge of God. Bahá’u’lláh tells Salmán that the door of the Ancient Being is closed to all, yet that the knowledge of these sanctified Beings has been made identical with the knowledge of God Himself. Even then the knower’s capacity sets limits, and the seeker who flies through all that can be known reads only the letters of his own self. Moses asked to see the divine glory and was shown goodness while direct vision was withheld [1]. The road leads on through the divine attributes present in every atom, through the Manifestation as the only route to knowledge of God, and into the names and attributes themselves.
subjects.arc: Enter through the mirror, look for signs in creation, and explore revelation as an opening toward the unknowable.

order.why: Look outward toward the traces of divine qualities.
shortened: But the question may be asked: How shall we know God? We know Him by His attributes. We know Him by His signs. We know Him by His names.

If we wish to come in touch with the reality of Divinity, we do so by recognizing its phenomena, its attributes and traces, which are widespread in the universe. All things in the world of phenomena are expressive of that one reality. Its lights are shining, its heat is manifest, its power is expressive, and its education, or training, resplendent everywhere.

order.why: Place the Manifestation within the account of signs throughout creation. Acknowledge the capacity and limits of the knower.
shortened: Knowing God, therefore, means the comprehension and knowledge of His attributes and not of His Reality. And even this knowledge of His attributes extends only as far as human power and capacity permit and remains wholly inadequate.

The knowledge of the reality of the Divinity is in no wise possible, but the knowledge of the Manifestations of God is the knowledge of God, for the bounties, splendours and attributes of God are manifest in them. Thus, whoso attains to the knowledge of the Manifestations of God attains to the knowledge of God, and whoso remains heedless of them remains bereft of that knowledge.

order.why: Begin with the mirror and sun as an accessible distinction.
shortened: It is clear, then, that the essential reality of God is revealed in His perfections; and the sun, with its perfections, reflected in a mirror, is a visible thing, an entity clearly expressing the bounty of God.

order.why: Clarify the distinction between attributes and Essence.
shortened: All things become known through knowledge, and no soul has ever known or will ever know that invisible Essence.
Therefore one must look to the attributes and signs, not to the Essence.

order.why: Explore the difficulty of applying human distinctions within God. Return to recognition of the divine Dawning-places.
shortened: Therefore the meaning of Knowing in this noble Tradition is not and never has been the knowledge of the true nature of the Absolute for that is beyond the province of Possible Being.  Rather it is the knowledge of the traces and effulgences of that Most Holy and Forbidden Mystery.  For however much detached minds and pure souls seek to penetrate the worlds of Inner Knowledge, their understanding will never penetrate more than that station which is a sign pointing towards the Monarch of Primal Oneness which He has placed as a trust within the reality of man.  And however much they may fly with triumphant wings in the limitless space of what is knowable and observable, they will read naught but the letters of the book of their own selves.

order.why: Explains why recognition of the unknowable Essence is attained through the Manifestation of its names and attributes.
Reconsider what seeing God can mean.
shortened: By seeing God is meant beholding the Manifestation of Himself; for witnessing the sun in its entire splendor, in a clear glassy surface, is identical with witnessing the essence of the sun itself.

order.why: Connect recognition with spiritual knowledge rather than prestige.
shortened: Man's highest station, however, is attained through faith in God in every Dispensation and by acceptance of what hath been revealed by Him, and not through learning; inasmuch as in every nation there are learned men who are versed in divers sciences. Nor is it attainable through wealth; for it is similarly evident that among the various classes in every nation there are those possessed of riches. Likewise are other transitory things.
True knowledge, therefore, is the knowledge of God, and this is none other than the recognition of His Manifestation in each Dispensation.

order.why: Return belief to the evidence of signs.
shortened: Whoso acknowledgeth belief in Him and in His signs and testimonies hath in truth acknowledged that which the Tongue of Grandeur uttered ere the creation of earth and heaven and the revelation of the Kingdom of Names.

order.why: Consider manifestation within creation.
shortened: Know thou that the One Essence, alone, without partner, is worthy of worship and none other. Whosoever worships His Essence without attention to aught else in His creation, and without desire for any recompense save Him, has truly worshipped God in the manner possible within the realm of contingency. One must be certain that the Essence in its essence was and is beyond description, recognition, or worship.
Rather, the way of worship is to worship Him according to how He has described Himself, without mention of aught else.

order.why: Read the language of first effulgence within this account.
shortened: Every mention of Thee, irrespective of the one who maketh it, must refer ultimately to the most exalted Word and the preexistent Pearl. This is none other than the Primal Will and the Original Point -- the initial indication of Thy Revelation and the first of Thine effulgences. This Thou didst generate of its own substance, and didst shed Thy splendor upon it through Thine all-glorious Name. Subsequently, the heavens shone forth with the light of Thy knowledge, and the earth was illumined with the rays of Thy countenance. Thou didst make this Point the very source of all creation, and the furthest Limit to which it may attain.

order.why: Close with the opening of a way where direct comprehension is closed.
shortened: O Salman! The door of the knowledge of the Ancient Being hath ever been, and will continue forever to be, closed in the face of men. No man’s understanding shall ever gain access unto His holy court. As a token of His mercy, however, and as a proof of His loving-kindness, He hath manifested unto men the Daystars of His divine guidance, the Symbols of His divine unity, and hath ordained the knowledge of these sanctified Beings to be identical with the knowledge of His own Self. Whoso recognizeth them hath recognized God.

order.why: Hear the recognition of signs in the language of prayer.
Encounter the relation of names to the Primal Will.

questions: What does the mirror image explain about knowing God, and what might be lost if we take the image too literally?
How do signs in creation and the qualities disclosed by a Manifestation relate within these passages?
What difference might recognizing a divine attribute make to the way we cultivate that quality in our own conduct?
How can increasing knowledge and increasing awareness of mystery develop together?

neighbors.invitation: Explore why receiving light does not amount to encompassing its source.
Consider how devotion relates to the qualities disclosed through a Manifestation.

references.label: 1 · Exodus 33:18–23 — glory, goodness, and the limits of vision
references.note: Moses asks to see divine glory; the answer speaks of goodness and a vision that is both granted and limited. Compare this narrative with the mirror metaphor, attending to what each text makes knowable and what each withholds.

subjects.introduction: A mirror cannot grow large enough to hold the sun, and this is no fault in the mirror. The Prophets, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá says, do not comprehend the Essence of God, since the lower can never encompass the higher, and Bahá’u’lláh pushes the thought to its limit: ten thousand prophets, each a Moses, stand thunderstruck on the Sinai of their search at the voice that says they shall never behold Him. That scene is drawn from the Qur’an, where Moses asks to see God and the mountain is crushed [1]; read in its own setting it holds both the longing and the limit. Bahá’u’lláh disclaims any grasp on God’s ultimate Will, and He prays that even the Manifestations, soaring as long as sovereignty endures, will fail to reach the precincts of the court of His knowledge. Water, fire, and the trumpet that wakes the dead pour from the divine Pen, and the Pen itself is beyond its readers. Such confessions do not close inquiry; they deepen devotion. The way continues into the relationship between the Manifestation and God, the limits of the intellect, and the transcendence that makes every nearness a gift.
subjects.arc: Move from the limits of a mirror to Sinai, then consider the humility and wonder of approaching what exceeds us.

order.why: Give that limit dramatic expression in the encounter at Sinai.
shortened: All the Embodiments of His Names wander in the wilderness of search, athirst and eager to discover His Essence, and all the Manifestations of His Attributes implore Him, from the Sinai of Holiness, to unravel His mystery.

Ten thousand Prophets, each a Moses, are thunderstruck upon the Sinai of their search at His forbidding voice, "Thou shalt never behold Me!"; whilst a myriad Messengers, each as great as Jesus, stand dismayed upon their heavenly thrones by the interdiction, "Mine Essence thou shalt never apprehend!"

order.why: Begin with the intelligible limit of a mirror’s capacity.
Widen the claim beyond any particular name or knower.
Explore its application even to the Prophets.
shortened: My inner and outer tongue, openly and secretly, testify that Thou hast been exalted above the reach and ken of Thy creatures, above the utterance of Thy servants, above the testimonies of Thy dear ones and Thy chosen ones, and the apprehension of Thy Prophets and of Thy Messengers.

order.why: Distinguish spiritual station from control over divine will.
Enter the language of water, fire, and the divine Pen.
Hear the Prophets’ confession of their limits.
shortened: The verse: "God would have you beware of Himself" unmistakably beareth witness to the reality of Our argument, and the words: "God was alone; there was none else besides Him" are a sure testimony of its truth. All the Prophets of God and their chosen Ones, all the divines, the sages, and the wise of every generation, unanimously recognize their inability to attain unto the comprehension of that Quintessence of all truth, and confess their incapacity to grasp Him, Who is the inmost Reality of all things.

order.why: Directly states that all Prophets acknowledge their powerlessness to know the divine Essence and all Messengers confess their inability to comprehend it.
Encounter the passage’s account of recognition across Revelations.
shortened: Whoso beholdeth Me with an eye besides Mine own will never be able to know Me. None among the Manifestations of old, except to a prescribed degree, hath ever completely apprehended the nature of this Revelation.

order.why: Close with the unending reach of spiritual aspiration.
shortened: Wherefore, I bear witness with my soul, my spirit, my entire being, that should They Who are the Daysprings of Thy most holy unity and the Manifestations of Thy transcendent oneness be able to soar so long as Thine own sovereignty endureth and Thine all-compelling authority can last, they will fail in the end to attain unto even the precincts of the court wherein Thou didst reveal the effulgence of but one of Thy most mighty Names.

questions: What kinds of knowledge remain possible when comprehension of the divine Essence is said to be impossible?
How does the Sinai image express both the desire to know and the limits of the knower?
What difference is there between acknowledging mystery and using mystery to avoid careful thought?

neighbors.invitation: Explore the mirror as a means of recognition as well as an image of limitation.
Consider how the capacity to receive meaning may develop over time.

references.label: 1 · Qur’an 7:143 — Moses and the mountain
references.note: The encounter at the mountain gives a narrative setting for imagery used in these readings. Compare the desire for vision, the mountain’s collapse, and Moses’ response with the compilation’s account of divine transcendence. What becomes clearer when the allusion is read in its own setting?

subjects.introduction: Four stations: divinity, prophethood, sanctification, servitude. Four aspects of a single name. Four essences, directions, streams, and days. Four pillars of religion in the Báb’s early writing, unity, prophethood, guardianship, and the community of the faithful, each gate unsound without the last. The number keeps returning, and the temptation is to treat it as a master key. The Writings themselves ask for something slower: each fourfold pattern organises a different field, some are explained, one is openly debated among learned men, and one belongs to a mystical language of the Point and the letters that circle it. Held apart, the patterns become a real question about how sacred order helps memory and contemplation, and about what further study a symbol needs before it can be interpreted. The foursquare city of Revelation, measured with its twelve gates and foundations, shows another tradition giving holiness a numbered shape [1]. From here the path leads back into Islam, where the Báb’s pillars have their roots, into the person of Muḥammad, and into the degrees of divine unity that the first pillar, tawḥíd, names.
subjects.arc: Start with an explicit fourfold pattern, compare its different uses, and explore the possibilities and limits of sacred symbolism.

order.why: Begin with four named spiritual stations.
shortened: The first station is the station of Divinity; the second is the station of Prophethood or Manifestation; the third is the station of Sanctification and the fourth is the station of Servitude."

order.why: Connects the four pillars with successive stations of unity, prophethood, divine authority and the followers, then gives the four corresponding declarations.
Compare a different fourfold account of identity.
Broaden the field to elements, directions, and streams.
shortened: So, the four essences, four directions, four streams, four streets, four stations and four days are much mentioned in the words of the ancestors and those who lived in former times. When on the fourth day, the sun, the star of the fourth heaven, faces the fourth station, every one who is godly will return to God and every one who is ungodly will return to the Evil One.

order.why: Read the Báb’s account of religious pillars in its own terms.
shortened: Having understood this noble premise, know that this upright religion also has four pillars: The first pillar is Unity (Tawhid), the second is Prophethood, the third is Guardianship, and the fourth is the Shi'a.

order.why: Place the reported criticism beside the particular tradition it concerns.
shortened: Haji Murtada has written that however much we studied the books, we could not find the source of the Fourth Pillar except in the book of some Indian person who wrote "The Fourth Pillar is in the impurities..."

order.why: Encounter a more compressed use of the pillar image.
Links the four pillars to a prayer for recognition of the Door of the divine Proof.
Consider the interdependence of the four religious terms.
shortened: And verily religion is established upon four pillars: the unity of God [al-tawhid], the reality of prophethood [al-nubuwwa], the succession of authority [al-walaya], and the community of followers [al-shi'a]: four gates, the first of which cannot be sound without the last.

order.why: Explains the four supports through their associated declarations and symbolic colors.
Close with the mystical language of the Point and its pillars.
shortened: Praise be to God Who created the Point and appointed for it four pillars, and brought forth from the first pillar an Alif which spoke of its own self and circled round it, being the mirror reflecting it in the station of Oneness, wherein the believers profess His unity, the sincere ones glorify Him, and those nigh unto God proclaim that He is God, there is none other God but Him, the All-Knowing, the One. And from its second pillar He manifested that same Form in another station, and shed upon it the lights shining forth from His Most Great Horizon, whereupon it called out, turned towards Him, arose in the station of multiplicity, and proclaimed that verily there is none other God but Him, the Mighty, the Bestower.

And from its third pillar He brought forth another Alif and made it the Dawning-Place of His most exalted attributes, and it proclaimed that verily there is none other God but Him, the Mighty, the All-Knowing. And from its fourth pillar He manifested that which reflected the first, third and second pillars, and it proclaimed in this station that He is the First and the Last, the Manifest and the Hidden, there is none other God but Him, the Mighty, the Peerless.

questions: What work does the fourfold pattern perform in each passage, and where do the meanings diverge?
What evidence would be needed to move from noticing a recurring number to claiming a shared doctrine?
How might a symbol guide contemplation while still calling for historical and linguistic study?

neighbors.invitation: Follow the symbolic use of letters and numbers into questions of interpretation.
Compare a clearly defined fourfold explanation with the several symbolic patterns here.

references.label: 1 · Revelation 21:12–16 — the measured city
references.note: The city’s gates, foundations, and equal dimensions give sacred order a spatial form. Compare the role of number here with the differing fourfold structures in the compilation. Similar forms invite comparison, but do not by themselves establish identical meanings or a historical connection.

subjects.introduction: Tie ten bars of iron together as tightly as you like and they remain ten bars. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá uses the image to show that real unity comes only through fire: in the furnace the metals melt, their atoms flow together, and a single casting emerges from the mould. Iron thrust into flame loses its coldness, blackness and hardness and takes on the heat and glow of the fire, and a soul consumed in the love of God is changed in the same way, until it sees and hears by a light not its own. The old alchemical dream of dyeing metals is reread as the adorning of pure hearts with the color of God. Malachi pictured a refiner bent over silver until it was fit for a righteous offering [1]; in both visions the heat serves what it brings forth. Even teaching a single soul is likened to turning black stone into diamond and base metal into gold. The way runs on into the lore of alchemy, the search for the elixir, and the wider language of symbols.
subjects.arc: Begin with bars that cannot be united by tying, then explore purification, illumination, and the transformation of hearts.

order.why: Concise authorized interplay between testing gold and being tested by gold.
Open with the memorable difference between tying bars and melting metal.
shortened: If you take ten bars of iron and tie them together no matter how closely they will not become one, but when a metallurgist comes on the scene, he takes the ten bars, melt them in the furnace and cast them in one mould. Only through this fiery process their atoms will flow and commingle with each other, becoming united and inseparable!

order.why: Casting differing religious communities in a single mold as an image of unity.
Examine purification through the crucible.
shortened: But the only way to make these metals into one alloy, is to put them into a crucible and apply intense heat to melt them all.

order.why: Authorized concrete application of separating gold from dross through tests.
Distinct workshop and crucible image of the purpose of earthly life.
Consider the qualities acquired by iron in fire.
Let a second source develop the image of glowing iron.
Authorized explanation of sacrifice through iron assuming the qualities of fire.
States an essential limit of the iron-and-fire analogy: contingency cannot become divine essence.
Compact sustained metaphor of the heart as retort and love as fire.
Extended authorized spiritual interpretation of sulphur, mercury and the philosopher’s stone.
Authorized developed copper-to-gold analogy explicitly applied to transformation through faith.
Turn attention from changing materials to changing hearts.
shortened: And by this dyeing was not meant, and is not meant, the dyeing of metals, but rather the adorning of pure hearts with the dye of God, and that is the sanctification and purification of souls from the various colors of the world.

order.why: Defines effective teaching through spiritual transmutation and metallurgy.
Close with teaching understood as spiritual transmutation.
Authorized prayer employing the divine elixir metaphor.

questions: What distinguishes outward association from the inward unity suggested by the metal images?
How do purification, illumination, and transmutation illuminate different aspects of spiritual growth?
Where does the comparison with metal cease to help, especially when we consider freedom, diversity, and the manner of teaching?

neighbors.invitation: Explore the difference between formal civility and sincere fellowship.
Place the desire to transform hearts beside respect for another person’s response.

references.label: 1 · Malachi 3:2–3 — the refiner’s work
references.note: Malachi connects the refining of silver and gold with purification for righteous offering. Compare that purpose with the compilation’s images of unity and transformed character. What makes the heat meaningful in each text?

subjects.displayTitle: When the last become the first
subjects.introduction: Rank is a fragile thing in the Day of God. Bahá’u’lláh declares that the highest among the people have been made lowest and the lowest highest, and He calls this the mystery of the Great Reversal in the Sign of the Sovereign. Learned men who believed they had climbed to the summit of knowledge stayed veiled from the Sun of Truth, while souls whose names no one had ever mentioned heard the call and answered it. A shepherd is remembered before the Throne; the owner of earthly treasure is forgotten. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá adds that divine tests always bring down the great and raise the lowly, as every past Manifestation has shown. Mary sang of the mighty cast down and the humble lifted up [1], and her song belongs to the same long overturning. For anyone proud of position or discouraged by obscurity, the teaching cuts both ways. It also opens toward the hidden language of letters, numbers and symbols in which such mysteries are written, and toward the convulsions of a world whose old order of greatness is being shaken.
subjects.arc: Start with unexpected recognition, reconsider familiar rankings, and discover the possibilities concealed in modest beginnings.

order.why: Place that contrast within the larger language of reversal.
shortened: Regard thou, O friend, the mystery of the Great Reversal in the Sign of the Sovereign. Through this reversal He hath caused the exalted to be abased and the abased to be exalted.

order.why: Begin with recognition by the unknown and exclusion through learned pride.
shortened: This is a Day wherein God hath made the highest among the people lowest, and the lowest highest. Observe how many souls who deemed themselves to have ascended to the loftiest heights of knowledge and learning remained yet veiled from the Sun of Truth, while how many whose names were never mentioned, after the call of the Lord of Names was raised between earth and heaven, turned to the most exalted horizon and quaffed the purest wine.

order.why: Direct explanation of the named mystery, with the reversal of learned and unlearned at the Manifestation.
Direct explanation linking the great reversal to transformed spiritual heavens and recognition.
Consider the searching effect of spiritual tests.
shortened: This is the truth. But we must know also that in the divine tests, changes always come; the great among us have to fall down, and the low ones have to rise. This has been shown in all the Manifestations of the past. In the Koran it says that when the great test comes, the high will fall low, and the low will rise high...

order.why: Let the elevation of the lowly recur from another source.
shortened: This is a Day wherein We have made the highest among the people their lowest, and their lowest their highest, and We have made those who were oppressed the inheritors of the Kingdom, even as We promised them aforetime.

order.why: Hear the reversal through its traditional religious language.
shortened: This is why it was said aforetime: "We shall make their highest ones their lowest ones, and their lowest ones their highest ones."

order.why: Examine the contrast between outward glory and admission to the divine court.
shortened: The shepherd hath been mentioned before the Throne, while forgotten was he who possessed the treasures of the earth and enjoyed a mighty portion. This is a Day wherein We have made the highest among the people lowest, and the lowest highest. Thy Lord, verily, is the Almighty, the Powerful. How many were possessed of glory who were turned away from the door, and how many were abased who entered and attained, exclaiming: "Praise be to God Who hath made me to achieve this noble vision!"

questions: Which measures of importance do these passages unsettle, and what qualities do they invite us to notice instead?
How might learning or reputation become a veil, and how could the same resources be used in service?
What would change in a community that expected significant insight and initiative from people easily overlooked?

neighbors.invitation: Explore a way of sharing conviction without claiming personal superiority.
Consider how a small group might understand its capacity without measuring it by numbers alone.

references.label: 1 · Luke 1:46–55 — Mary’s song
references.note: Mary’s song joins gratitude with the reversal of social expectations: the lowly are raised and the hungry fed. Compare this with the compilation’s emphasis on spiritual recognition. Where do the social and inward dimensions of reversal meet?

subjects.introduction: Nobody chooses to fall asleep, and nobody escapes death; ‘Abdu’l-Bahá begins from such plain compulsions to show that the whole contingent world lives under a law it did not make. Everything we meet is dependent, limited, divisible, caused, and that dependence points to a reality that is none of these things: the Necessary Being, self-sufficient and without beginning, whose perfection is the measure of our imperfection. The vocabulary gets precise along the way. The existence we can conceive in the mind is itself only an accident of things, not that real Existence through which all things are realized; a chair is originated because it has a cause, which is a different matter from having begun at some moment in time; and to call creation nothing beside God is to speak relatively, for even a stone has being, and created things are not parts of God but realities He has made. Aquinas, arguing from the possible to the necessary, follows a path that can be walked step by step beside these claims [1]. The road leads on to existence and nonexistence, to preexistence and eternity, and to the relation of essence to substance and form.
subjects.arc: Enter through ordinary dependence, clarify different senses of existence, and investigate the relation of creation to its source.

order.why: Concise account of contingent existence depending on the outpouring of Necessary Being.
Begin with familiar signs of dependence, including sleep and change.
shortened: It is certain that the entire contingent world is subject to an order and a law which it can never disobey. Even man is forced to submit to death, sleep, and other conditions-that is, in certain matters he is compelled, and this very compulsion implies the existence of One Who is All-Compelling. So long as the contingent world is characterized by dependency, and so long as this dependency is one of its essential requirements, there must be One Who in His own Essence is independent of all things.

order.why: Develop the contrast between contingent limitation and necessary perfection.
Explains why the knowledge of Necessary Being cannot be made dependent on objects as the knowledge of contingent beings is.
Give the distinction a more exact theological form.
Separate true existence from a concept shared in thought. Encounter the technical language of substance and accident.
shortened: But the truly learned among the Theosophists and Sufis have concluded, after deep consideration of this matter, that there are two kinds of existence. One kind is this common existence which is conceived by the mind of man. This existence is originated and is an accident among others, whereas the realities of things are the substances. But what is meant by unity of existence is not this commonly perceived existence, but that real Existence which is sanctified and exalted above all expression, an Existence through which all things are realized. This Existence is one; it is that One through which all things---such as matter, energy, and that common existence which is conceived by the human mind---have come to exist.

order.why: Hear dependence expressed through prayer.
shortened: Who is there, O my Lord, that, when Thou revealest the first glimmerings of the signs of Thy transcendent sovereignty and might, hath the power to claim for himself any existence whatever? Existence itself is as nothing when brought face to face with the mighty and manifold wonders of Thine incomparable Self.

order.why: Continue that devotional response to necessary being.
Distinguish causal origination from a temporal beginning.
shortened: Essential pre-existence is an existence which is not preceded by a cause; essential origination is preceded by a cause. Temporal pre-existence has no beginning; temporal origination has both a beginning and an end. For the existence of each and every thing depends upon four causes: the efficient cause, the material cause, the formal cause and the final cause. So this chair has a creator who is a carpenter, a matter which is wood, a form which is that of a chair, and a purpose which is to serve as a seat. Therefore, this chair is essentially originated, for it is preceded by, and its existence is conditioned upon, a cause.

order.why: Consider division and descent as marks of contingency.
Preserve the distinction between the two modes of existence.
shortened: Existence is of two kinds: One is the existence of the True One (God) which is sanctified above the comprehension of creation. He is the Unknowable Invisible. He is not preceded by any cause, but rather is the Creator of the Cause of causes. He is Ancient without beginning and absolutely Self-Sufficient. The second existence is that of creation. It is a general existence which is a mental concept that human reason can comprehend. This existence is originated, dependent, preceded by cause, and contingent. Therefore, the contingent cannot become ancient, and the ancient cannot become contingent. Creation cannot become Creator, and the Creator cannot become creation. The transformation of essence is impossible in the realm of existence.

order.why: Consider the relation of the preexistent Sun to its rays.
shortened: And regarding proof for the temporal eternity of contingent beings in this transient world - briefly, divine sovereignty is eternal, and the existence of beings is from the eternal effulgences of the Sun of Reality. One cannot imagine the sun without rays. All divine names and attributes are eternal, and their requirements are also eternal. This is a brief answer - reflect upon it to derive detailed meanings, as there is no opportunity for elaboration.

order.why: Examine conceptual and external existence.
Close by clarifying the reality and distinctness of created beings.
shortened: Compared to God nothing has existence but this does not mean that even stones do not have being. It is speaking relatively. Moreover, God reveals Himself in all things in the sense that He is the source of their being and the Cause of their existence. Without Him all things will shrink down into nothing. This however does not mean that all things are parts of God as the pantheist believes. The pantheist says that only God exists, objects are mere modes of His attributes. Baha'u'llah however says that objects have a separate reality that is created by God.

questions: Which experiences of dependence make the distinction between necessary and contingent being intelligible, and what further argument does it require?
How is dependence on a cause different from having a beginning at a particular time?
What does it mean to call created existence relative without dismissing the world as unreal?
How might the philosophical argument and the prayers affect one another when read together?

neighbors.invitation: Use the chair and its four causes to examine different forms of dependence.
Explore the relation between knowledge and the realities known.

references.label: 1 · Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I, question 2, article 3
references.note: Read the third way, which argues from possibility and necessity. Set out its steps beside the compilation’s arguments from dependence and limitation. Where do they follow similar paths, and which premises or meanings of necessity require separate examination?

subjects.introduction: Say the Name of God when trouble comes, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá advised, when someone opposes you, and even in the middle of your work. In the Kitáb-i-Aqdas Bahá’u’lláh ordains a simple daily act: having washed the hands and face, to sit, turn to God, and repeat Alláh-u-Abhá ninety-five times. Around that discipline gather other uses of the Greatest Name, recited at morning to apprehend hidden mysteries, spoken in silence to bring harmony into a meeting, and exchanged as a greeting that, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá wrote, filled His soul with fragrance whenever it reached His ears. The Qur’an likewise calls believers to remember God often [1], morning and evening. Repetition here is not mechanical. It trains the heart to return, again and again, to the One it loves, until remembrance colours the whole day. From this practice the way leads to the Greatest Name itself and its meanings, to the laws of the Aqdas, and to the quieter work of meditation.
subjects.arc: Begin with remembrance amid difficulty, explore its daily discipline, and consider how devotion enters ordinary encounters.

order.why: Present the prescribed daily practice and its stated preparation.
Start where a reader may need remembrance most: trouble or demanding work.
shortened: If you fall into trouble say "Ya Baha'u'l Abha"; and if anyone oppose you, say "Ya Baha ul Abha" Even when you may be in your work, mention "Ya Baha ul Abha."

order.why: A Babi ordinance on repeating divine names ninety-five times, with its stated purpose of recognition at the next Revelation.
Directly answers whether ablutions must be renewed before the ninety-five recitations of the Greatest Name.
Reinforce the place of remembrance in the day.
Uses changing the prescribed number of recitations as a concrete example of introducing division under a religious pretext.
Connect the practice with morning.
Retain the second morning counsel as a separate voice.
Read the reported gathering’s practice in its particular setting.
shortened: We asked 'Abdu'l-Baha about our Oakland, home meetings - how they should be conducted and we told him we opened our service by saying the Greatest Name (in silence) nine times. He replied, That is very good, that is right for that brings harmony into the meeting.

order.why: Explore the devotional meaning of a greeting.
shortened: Concerning the greeting which thou didst mention, this servant's heart and soul desire that the blessed Name alone may be the spiritual fragrance of the sincere ones in the gardens of the earthly and heavenly kingdoms. And when this holy Name reaches my ears, my soul becomes filled with spirit and sweet fragrance, and my spirit is moved. Therefore, O friend, seek what brings joy to my heart and soul, and raise such a cry of "Allah-u-Abha" that it may reach the ears of all the sincere ones here and gladden the heart of this servant.

order.why: Close with the stated universal application of the daily recitation.

questions: How might repeated words deepen attention, and what helps keep a familiar practice alive?
What difference does it make to distinguish a prescribed daily observance from a practice described for a particular gathering?
How could remembrance shape the way we begin work, meet difficulty, or greet another person?

neighbors.invitation: Explore the deliberate turning of attention at the beginning of a day.
Continue the rhythm of remembrance into the night.

references.label: 1 · Qur’an 33:41 — frequent remembrance
references.note: Read this invitation to frequent remembrance, then follow the link to verse 42, which names morning and evening. Compare that daily rhythm with the compilation’s specific practice and its spontaneous invocations. What relationships emerge between regularity, freedom, and attention?

subjects.displayTitle: Prayer at the beginning of the day
subjects.introduction: Before the day has made its claims, there is an hour that belongs to God. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá writes that one who remembers the All-Merciful at daybreak, with melodious voice, will find a new spirit and fresh confirmations, and He asks His friends to set their faces consciously toward the Kingdom at every dawn. The Báb gives a prayer of glorification to be said each morning, and another prayer remembers God at evening with those near Him and calls upon Him at dawn with the melodies of the sincere. To two daughters of a martyr, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá offers words for their morning praise; to others He sends a hope that the confirmations of Bahá’u’lláh might surge like the sea. The psalmist, too, lifts his voice in the morning and waits in expectation [1]. Dawn prayer is a beginning that sets the course, and it opens into the wide world of prayer, in all its forms, that can sustain a whole life.
subjects.arc: Open with the freshness of dawn, turn toward a purpose, and carry the morning’s prayer into the unfolding day.

order.why: An explicit morning thanksgiving for awakening from sleep, with the face turned toward the Daystar of Revelation.
Begin with dawn as a source of fresh spirit and song.
Make the turning of attention deliberate.
shortened: O servant of God! At the break of every morn, set thy face consciously toward the Kingdom of God, and humbly offer this supplication:
Thou beareth witness, O my God, that I desire to behold Thy lights and long to apprehend Thy mysteries.

order.why: Give that orientation a personal voice of hope.
shortened: In the evening, O my God, I remember Thee with the hosts of those near unto Thee, and at dawn I call upon Thee, O my Hope, with the melodies of the sincere ones.

order.why: Connect renewal with sustained effort in prayer.
shortened: Strive with all thy power in prayers and communions at the hour of dawn to increase thine alertness day by day, to strip away the misgivings that veil the people of doubt and lead them towards the Most Great Guide with the potent knowledge of God so that like unto a candle thou mayest illuminate every meeting with the light of recognition.

order.why: Hear morning glorification in a prayer of the Báb.
A prayer explicitly offered on this morning, asking for nearness, recognition and what benefits this world and the next.
Present the counsel to recite at dawn without inventing a specified prayer.
shortened: And Thou hast commanded all to recite it at dawn, that none among those endowed with vision might be debarred therefrom.

order.why: Read the encouragement to particular bereaved relatives in its personal setting.
Explore the direction and feeling of a morning prayer.
shortened: At every instant, I beg for you assistance, bounty, and a fresh favor and blessing, so that the confirmations of Baha'u'llah may, like unto the sea, be constantly surging, the lights of the Sun of Truth may shine upon you all and that ye may be confirmed in service, may become the manifestations of bounty and that each one of you may, at dawn, turn unto the Holy Land and may experience spiritual emotions with all intensity.

questions: What might change when the beginning of a day is understood as an opportunity for renewal?
How do the different prayers and personal counsels enlarge our understanding of a shared devotional practice?
How could an intention formed at dawn become visible in the way we respond to someone later in the day?

neighbors.invitation: Follow prayer into moments of work and difficulty.
Explore the act of turning toward God before speaking or serving.

references.label: 1 · Psalm 5:1–3 — prayer in the morning
references.note: The speaker brings words, meditation, and a cry for help into the morning. Compare this expectant address with the compilation’s images of renewal. How do speaking, listening, and waiting belong together at the start of a day?

subjects.displayTitle: Prayer in the evening and night
subjects.introduction: When the eyes of the world close, the eyes of the worshipper open. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá describes prayer in the middle of the night as sweet, delicious, satisfying, a time when the ears of the devotee are tuned to a music no one else is awake to hear. Evening has its own place in that rhythm: Bahá’u’lláh remembers God at evening with the hosts of those near to Him and calls on Him again at dawn, and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá advises that whoever wishes to pray at dawn should begin with supplications the evening before. The night is also a place of collective memory. Bahá’u’lláh and the Báb composed prayers for particular sacred nights, long litanies that recall the deliverance of Adam, Noah, Abraham, and Moses, or that call down every glory upon the Tree of God, and the vigil becomes a festival. The psalmist, too, remembers God upon his bed and meditates in the night watches, satisfied as with marrow and fatness [1]. An evening practice carries something into the next morning. From here the path widens into the whole treasury of prayer for every hour and need.
subjects.arc: Begin with evening remembrance, enter the stillness of night, and let the vigil open toward another dawn.

order.why: Turn to a prayer expressly introduced for midnight.
Start with the simple invitation to remember at evening.
shortened: In the evening, O my God, I remember Thee with the hosts of those near unto Thee, and at dawn I call upon Thee, O my Hope, with the melodies of the sincere ones.

order.why: Complete short prayer expressly for lying down to sleep.
Specific preparation for prayer before sleep and vision.
Explore the sweetness attributed to night prayer.
shortened: How sweet, how delicious, how satisfying, how spiritual is prayer in the middle of nights! While all the eyes are closed, the eyes of the worshipper are wide open. While all the ears are stopped, the ears of the devotee are attuned to the Subtle music of God! While the majority of the people are fast sleep, the adorer of the Ideal Beloved is wakeful.

order.why: Connect the evening’s preparation to the next morning.
shortened: When you desire to engage in prayers at dawn, you must recite supplications from the Supreme Pen in the evening and at sunrise.

order.why: Enter the setting of a particular sacred vigil and its remembered deliverances.
Read the Báb’s prayer within its specified observance.
Close by joining night and day in continuing invocation.

questions: What does the atmosphere of night make possible in prayer that may be harder to notice during the day?
How do personal devotion and the remembrance of sacred events illuminate each other here?
What might an evening practice carry forward into the next morning?

neighbors.invitation: Follow the night’s preparation into the renewal of dawn.
Consider how particular moments belong to a continuing pattern of devotion.

references.label: 1 · Psalm 63:5–8 — remembrance in the night watches
references.note: The psalm links night remembrance with nourishment, joy, and reliance on divine help. Compare its imagery with the sweetness of prayer in these selections. How can stillness become an active form of turning toward God?

subjects.introduction: Before the first mouthful, a pause. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá asks that the food be made heavenly and that those seated around it become life-giving to the world, so that an ordinary supper opens onto the Supreme Concourse and the strength it gives is already pointed toward service. Thanks at table is never only about the plate. It notices the earth, the rain and the many hands that brought the meal this far, and then it admits that the giving runs further than any thanks can reach; the finite cannot keep pace with the Infinite, and so the prayer ends not in settlement but in asking for more. Deuteronomy adds a sober warning for the well fed: satisfaction has a way of persuading us that our own hand produced the plenty [1]. Gratitude that remembers its source turns into hospitality, and the habit of pausing to give thanks at meals leads naturally into the wider life of prayer, where every need and every gift find their words.
subjects.arc: Begin with a shared meal, follow nourishment into service, and reflect on a gratitude larger than repayment.

order.why: Explore the image of heavenly nourishment.
Begin with food shared and a prayer that widens its meaning.
shortened: O Lord! Make this food heavenly and make those assembled here of the hosts of Thy Supreme Concourse so that they may become life-giving and the cause of the enlightenment of the world of man, that they may arise to, guide all the peoples of the world.

order.why: An actual supplication with instructions for entering the Unity Feast.
Connect the strength received at a table to service.
shortened: My Lord and My Hope! Praise be to Thee that Thou hast sent down upon us this spiritual table, this divine bounty, this heavenly blessing. O our Lord, enable us to eat of this food of the kingdom that its subtle essences may pervade the corners of our spiritual being and that there may be produced from that heavenly strength for the service of Thy cause, the spread of Thy revelation, and the adorning of Thy garden with lofty trees bearing branches near at hand, perfumed with fresh breezes.

order.why: End with bounty exceeding the measure of our gratitude.

questions: How do these prayers connect bodily nourishment with spiritual purpose?
What might gratitude at a meal help us notice about the people, land, and labor that sustain us?
How could the strength received at a table become hospitality or service offered to others?

neighbors.invitation: Explore the value of welcome and companionship around a simple meal.
Consider the labor and knowledge through which food becomes a shared source of comfort.

references.label: 1 · Deuteronomy 8:10–18 — remembering after abundance
references.note: The passage links thanks after eating with the danger of attributing prosperity entirely to one’s own power. Read it beside the prayers’ sense of unrepayable bounty, considering how satisfaction might deepen responsibility rather than forgetfulness.

subjects.introduction: Sacrifice begins more quietly than its fiercest images suggest: in a prayer for deeds that spread the fragrance of God’s good pleasure, and in a plea for contentment, patience under decree, and fortitude in tribulation. From there the language of devotion deepens, asking for self-surrender, steadfast loyalty, and reliance upon God alone. One prayer begs that its speaker’s life be offered for the lovers of God and the body become dust on the path they tread; another remembers those who surrendered their spirits in His love, and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá asks that the yearners be raised to life on the martyr’s field. Such longing reaches toward a life without end, not toward death for its own sake. Paul’s appeal to present one’s body as a living offering gives a related sense of a life given wholly to God [1]. What is surrendered becomes a source of life for others. That discovery leads on to martyrs and martyrdom, to the meaning of tests and trials, and to the mystery of sacrifice.
subjects.arc: Begin with good deeds and patience, approach the language of martyrdom in its devotional setting, and reflect on a life of dedication.

order.why: Explore surrender and faithfulness.
shortened: Ordain for me and him sacrifice in the field of self-surrender, steadfastness in loyalty, independence from all else save Thee, orientation toward Thee, reliance upon Thee, and martyrdom in Thy presence. By Thy glory! This is the ultimate hope and supreme aspiration of my heart, O Thou Lord of glory and perfection! Verily, Thou art the All-Glorious, the Most High.

order.why: Establish good deeds as an immediate form of assistance and dedication.
shortened: I beseech Thee by the ocean of Thy verses and the lights of Thy Throne to aid me to perform such deeds as will diffuse the fragrance of Thy good-pleasure.

order.why: Ground sacrifice in patience, contentment, and fortitude.
shortened: Our Lord! Ordain for us goodly contentment, patience under decree, fortitude in tribulation, and precedence to the field of sacrifice in the court of grandeur.

order.why: Introduce the devotional image of following the Beloved.
shortened: O God, give us to drink from the same cup that thou hast ordained for the Most Great Name and make us inebriated with that wine that we might follow the path of that Beloved of all and ascend unto thy Kingdom.

order.why: Remember those who suffered death for their allegiance.
shortened: I beseech Thee to adorn this servant with the ornament of faithfulness amidst the concourse of creation, in such wise that Thou mayest make me one of those who have been martyred in Thy path and who have surrendered their spirits in Thy love and good-pleasure.

order.why: Read the intense prayer in the light of that remembrance.
Asks to be among those who sacrifice their souls and possessions in God's path, within a prayer of gratitude and reliance.
Consider the prayer’s horizon of enduring life.
shortened: O Lord! Ordain for me this supreme bounty and grant me this mighty gift, that I may attain unto everlasting and eternal life that hath no end. Verily, Thou art the Gracious, the Merciful, the All-Bountiful."

order.why: A brief prayer that joins sacrifice of self with service to humanity and fellowship between hearts.
End with the most searching devotional language, held within the compilation’s wider account of steadfastness.
shortened: O Divine Providence! Lift to Thy lovers' lips a cup brimful of anguish. To the yearners on Thy pathway, make sweetness but a sting, and poison honey-sweet. Set Thou our heads for ornaments on the points of spears. Make Thou our hearts the targets for pitiless arrows and darts. Raise Thou this withered soul to life on the martyr's field, make Thou his faded heart to drink the draught of tyranny, and thus grow fresh and fair once more.

questions: How do the opening passages on deeds and patience shape your reading of the later prayers?
What forms can the surrender of self-interest take in an ordinary life of responsibility and service?
How might a community honor the steadfastness of persecuted people while working to protect life and relieve suffering?
What does the comparison with a living offering add to reflection on dedication, endurance, and hope?

neighbors.invitation: Explore the transformation of struggle into construction and illumination.
Consider the motives that sustain service beyond personal recognition or reward.

references.label: 1 · Romans 12:1–2 — a living offering
references.note: Paul joins the offering of one’s embodied life with a renewed mind. Compare this Christian appeal with the compilation’s range from good deeds to prayers shaped by persecution. What forms of daily dedication become visible through the comparison?

subjects.displayTitle: The living waters of the Word
subjects.introduction: A spring can run close beneath the surface and still be choked. Bahá’u’lláh warns against obstructing the luminous spring of the soul with the thorns and brambles of vain affection, and from that image a whole way of teaching unfolds. Water is received before it is given: drink as much as you can from the cup of God’s love, then cause others to drink. Detachment lets the waters of wisdom gush from a heart; joy and daily renewal make a person a spring from which other souls can be quickened; a single handful from the living ocean, sprinkled with the hand of detachment, is enough to enrich all who exist. At the well in Samaria, a request for a drink turns into the promise of water springing up within a person [1], the same movement from thirst to life, from receiving to sharing. Finally the teacher is only a reed through which the Holy Spirit reaches a seeking soul. Pursuing that image leads to the water of life itself, to what it means to be a channel for the Spirit, and to the enkindlement that keeps the channel clear.
subjects.arc: Clear the spring’s channel, receive its refreshment, and explore the humility of helping living water reach another person.

order.why: Begin with the blocked channel and the work of clearing it.
Join receiving the water to sharing it.
shortened: Drink thou as much as thou canst from this overflowing cup of the love of God and then cause others to drink; take thou a portion from this ocean of guidance and then suffer others to share.

order.why: Connect detachment with the flow of wisdom.
shortened: God will, no doubt, inspire whosoever detacheth himself from all else but Him, and will cause the pure waters of wisdom and utterance to gush out and flow copiously from his heart.

order.why: Connects continually drinking and giving others the life-giving water with the concrete service of teaching.
Turn toward the spring within.
Explore the water’s power to quicken.
Explains why people should teach even though the Cause does not need their assistance: to quicken souls with living waters.
Explains that thirst must first be awakened through conduct and character before the water of life can be offered.
Emphasize the joy of offering it to others.
shortened: How happy he who proffers freely the cup of everlasting life to others! How joyous the pure-hearted one who would unloose his tongue and shed the generous jewels of utterance before such souls as are prepared to receive them!

order.why: Give the image a particular setting of service and renewal.
Consider the heart as a receptacle for the ocean.
shortened: I implore Thee, by Thy Name which none hath befittingly recognized, and whose import no soul hath fathomed; I beseech Thee, by Him Who is the Fountain-Head of Thy Revelation and the Day-Spring of Thy signs, to make my heart to be a receptacle of Thy love and of remembrance of Thee. Knit it, then, to Thy most great Ocean, that from it may flow out the living waters of Thy wisdom and the crystal streams of Thy glorification and praise.

order.why: Explore the abundance held in a drop.
shortened: O thou who journeyest unto God! Take thy portion from this ocean and deprive not thyself of that which hath been ordained therein, and be of them that attain. Were all who are in the heavens and earth to be given but a drop thereof, they would find themselves enriched through the enrichment of God, the Powerful, the All-Knowing, the All-Wise. Take, with the hand of detachment, a handful from this Living Ocean, then sprinkle it upon all created things, that they may be purified from human limitations and be brought nigh unto the Most Sublime Vision of God, this hallowed and resplendent spot.

order.why: Connect spiritual learning with freedom from covetousness.
End with the reed as a reminder of the source of the teacher’s gift.

questions: What might obstruct the channel of spiritual receptivity, and how could it be cleared?
How does the image of water change our understanding of teaching and learning?
What helps a person share conviction generously while remembering that spiritual influence cannot be possessed?

neighbors.invitation: Explore an approach to teaching that remains generous whatever the response.
Consider how learning together changes the relation between teacher and learner.
